newsitem.title: UK: Austerity working for EMU convergence.
newsitem.headline: Austerity working for EMU convergence.

text.p: The fiscal austerity which countries have imposed upon themselves to meet entry targets for Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) in January 1999 seems to be working, a Reuters survey showed on Wednesday.

Forecasts from 35 economists across Europe showed on average that 14 out of 15 European Union (EU) countries were moving closer to achieving or bettering the Maastricht convergence targets set for membership of EMU.
But the forecasters in the quarterly survey, carried out between May 7 and 12, said Germany seems to have drifted further from meeting a key requirement.
According to the survey, the median of 29 forecasts for Germany's budget deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) ratio widened to 3.2 percent for 1997 compared with 3.05 percent three months ago.
It was the only average prediction in the entire survey which showed a drift away from the Maastricht targets compared with three months ago.
European nations hoping to qualify for EMU must aim at targets which cover budget deficits, debt, interest rates, inflation and currency stability.
The target budget deficit-to-GDP ratio of three percent or less in 1997 is proving to be a major stumbling block for Germany despite expenditure freezes.

"We expect a tax revenue shortfall this year and it will be difficult to implement further cuts given high levels of unemployment," said Gernot Nerb, senior economist at Salomon Brothers Germany. German national income and expenditure accounts are expected to be published on Thursday.
An end-1997 debt-to-GDP ratio of 62 percent, the median of 27 forecasts in the poll, also falls short of the 60 percent target, leaving it lacking in two out of the five criteria, the survey showed.
Predictions in the Reuters poll for Finland, Portugal and Britain showed the most improvement.
Finland, along with Luxembourg, is expected to meet all five criteria after the median forecast for its debt to GDP ratio fell to 60 percent from 61 percent in the previous survey.

"Finland was within the targets last year, but expenditure cuts implemented this year with good GDP growth are the main reasons for the expected improvement in total debt," said Juha Ahtola, chief economist at Merita Bank Finland.
Ahtola expects Finnish GDP to grow between a nominal five and six percent in 1997.
Both Britain and Portugal improved their predicted standings on budget deficit to GDP ratios, increasing to four from three the number of Maastricht criteria met.

Britain ranks alongside Luxembourg and Finland in meeting the economic criteria, the survey showed. But it fails to meet the currency stability target of being a member of the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM).
Britain's new Labour government is generally perceived to be more pro-Europe than the previous Conservative administration and analysts expect a slightly tighter fiscal stance.

"Activity levels, in terms of economic growth, are firmer and public borrowing is turning out better than we expected," said Nigel Richardson, international economist at Yamaichi International (Europe).

In the Nordic region, where public opinion and politicians remain divided over EMU and the single currency project, analysts expect Denmark to meet four of the Maastricht criteria and Sweden to meet three.
Both are expected to fail on the debt-to-GDP ratio and Sweden, like Britain, remains outside the ERM.

According to the average findings of the survey Italy, which is keen to join EMU in the first wave, is expected to fail both the budget deficit and debt criteria. Although some improvements have been made, they will will not be enough, analysts said.
"There is no proof it has achieved sustainable improvement and even after all these efforts, they will still have the worst deficit ratio within the EU," a Frankfurt-based economist said.
This is confirmed by the results of a monthly Reuters survey of EMU expectations, where only seven out of 49 contributors expect Italy to be included in the first wave.
Austria, Belgium, Ireland and the Netherlands are expected to meet all but the debt targets, according to the average of the forecasts in the survey.

France, although improving, is not forecast to meet the budget deficit yardstick. The median of 26 forecasts, at 3.05 percent, is 0.10 percentage points less than the average findings of the previous survey but still tantalisingly outside the Maastricht target.
All 20 contributors who made predictions for Greece said it would fail all convergence targets.
